course: Basic First Aid for Business and Community
module_title: Workplace and Community First Aid Preparedness

lessons.title: Conducting a First Aid Needs Assessment
lessons.body:
A first aid needs assessment is a simple survey to identify what could hurt people in your workplace or community, and what you need to respond. Start by walking through your siteâwhether it's a shop, farm, market stall, or community hall. List every possible hazard: sharp tools, hot cooking oil, chemicals, uneven floors, electrical wires, heavy sacks, and busy roads nearby. Also note who is present: staff, customers, children, elderly, or people with disabilities. For each hazard, ask: how likely is an injury, and how severe could it be? A cut from a knife is likely but usually minor; a fall from a roof is less likely but can be fatal.

Next, check legal requirements. In many African countries, labour laws require employers to provide first aid. For example, in Kenya, the Occupational Safety and Health Act (OSHA) 2007 requires workplaces to have a first aid kit and trained first aiders. In Nigeria, theFactories Act requires similar. Even if you are a small informal business, having a kit and a plan is good practice. Count your workers: for every 50 employees, at least one trained first aider is recommended. If you have 10 workers, aim for at least two trained people so someone is always available.

Now decide what supplies and training you need. If you work with chemicals, add eye wash and burn gel. If you work with machinery, add tourniquets and trauma dressings. If you are in a remote area, more supplies and training are needed because help may take hours. Also consider the distance to the nearest clinic or hospital. If it's more than 30 minutes away, you need more advanced supplies and someone trained in CPR and bleeding control.

Write down your findings in a simple table: hazard, who is at risk, what could happen, and what you will do. Review this assessment every year or when you change your activities. Share it with your team so everyone knows the risks and the plan. This assessment is the foundation for everything else in this module.

lessons.title: Building and Maintaining a First Aid Kit
lessons.body:
A first aid kit is not just a boxâit's a lifeline. For a small business or community group in Africa, you need a kit that handles common injuries: cuts, burns, fractures, and bites. Start with a sturdy, waterproof container with a handle. Label it clearly 'FIRST AID' and keep it in a known, accessible placeânot locked away. Check it monthly and restock after every use.

Here is a basic list for a workplace of 10-20 people: 20 adhesive bandages (plasters), 10 sterile gauze pads (4x4 inches), 2 rolls of medical tape, 1 roll of elastic bandage (for sprains), 1 triangular bandage (for slings), 1 pair of scissors, 1 tweezers, 5 pairs of disposable gloves, 1 CPR face shield, 1 instant cold pack, 1 thermometer, 1 bottle of antiseptic solution (like Dettol or Savlon), 1 tube of antibiotic ointment, 1 bottle of oral rehydration salts (ORS), 1 eye wash, 1 burn gel, 1 tourniquet (CAT or improvised), and a first aid manual. For larger sites or remote areas, add: splints, a space blanket, a flashlight, and a whistle.

In Africa, heat and humidity can ruin supplies. Store the kit in a cool, dry place. Replace expired itemsâcheck dates on antiseptics, ointments, and ORS. Latex gloves can degrade; consider nitrile. If you work with snakes or scorpions, add a snake bite kit (though most experts now advise against suction devices; instead include a compression bandage and a card with emergency numbers).

Keep a log sheet inside the kit. Every time you use an item, write it down. Every month, do a quick inventory. Every six months, do a full check. If you have multiple sites, each site needs its own kit. Train everyone on where the kit is and how to use basic items. A kit without training is just a box.

lessons.title: Developing Emergency Action Plans
lessons.body:
An Emergency Action Plan (EAP) is a written set of steps for what to do when someone is hurt or a disaster strikes. It answers: who calls for help, who gives first aid, who meets the ambulance, and where everyone goes. Without a plan, people freeze or panic. With a plan, they act.

Start by identifying the most likely emergencies: a worker cutting a hand, someone collapsing from heat stroke, a fire, a snake bite, or a road accident outside your gate. For each, write a simple sequence. For example, for a serious bleed: 1) Shout for the first aider. 2) Put on gloves. 3) Apply direct pressure with a clean cloth. 4) Do not remove the cloth; add more if needed. 5) Call the emergency number. 6) Keep the person lying down and warm. 7) Monitor breathing. 8) Hand over to medical help. Write these steps on a card and post them near the first aid kit.

Include important phone numbers: local ambulance, nearest clinic, police, fire, and a list of trained first aiders with their phone numbers. In many African communities, the nearest help might be a motorbike taxi or a private car. Identify a vehicle that can be used and a driver who is usually available. Also plan for communication: if phone networks are down, agree on a meeting point and a runner.

Assign roles: a First Aid Officer, a Caller, a Guide (to direct emergency services), and a Recorder (to write down what happened). Everyone should know their role. Practise the plan every three months with a simple drill. After any real incident, review the plan and improve it. Keep the plan simple, in local language, and accessible to all.

lessons.title: Training and Drills for Staff and Volunteers
lessons.body:
Training turns a first aid kit and plan into real action. Without practice, people forget. In Africa, where formal emergency services may be far away, trained staff and volunteers are often the only immediate help. Aim to train at least 10% of your team in basic first aid, and more if you are in a high-risk setting.

Basic first aid training should cover: how to check for danger, how to check responsiveness and breathing, how to call for help, how to do CPR, how to stop bleeding, how to treat burns, how to handle fractures, and how to treat shock. A good course lasts at least 6-8 hours and includes hands-on practice. Look for trainers from the Red Cross or St John Ambulance in your country. In Kenya, the Kenya Red Cross offers first aid courses; in Nigeria, the Nigerian Red Cross. Many offer short courses for workplaces. If you cannot afford a formal course, use free online videos and practice with your team, but be careful to follow current guidelines.

Drills are short practices of your Emergency Action Plan. Run a drill every three months. For example, simulate a worker collapsing. Have the team practise: who calls, who gives CPR, who meets the ambulance. Time how long it takes to get the first aider and the kit to the scene. After the drill, gather everyone and ask: what went well? What was confusing? What needs to change? Keep a record of drills.

Make training part of your routine. Put up posters showing CPR steps and bleeding control. Have a monthly 10-minute refresher at staff meetings. Celebrate those who complete training. Remember, a trained team saves lives and reduces panic. It also builds confidence and teamwork.

lessons.title: Incident Reporting and Documentation
lessons.body:
When an injury or near-miss happens, you must write it down. Incident reporting is not about blameâit's about learning and protecting your business and your people. A good report helps you see patterns, improve safety, and provide evidence if there is a legal claim.

Start with a simple incident report form. It should include: date, time, location, names of people involved, what happened, what injuries occurred, what first aid was given, who gave it, and what happened next (e.g., sent to clinic, went home). Also note the names of witnesses. Keep the form in a folder near the first aid kit. After any incident, the first aider or supervisor should fill it out within 24 hours. Be factual, not emotional. Write 'cut on left hand from knife' not 'careless worker cut himself'.

For serious incidentsâlike a broken bone, deep wound, or loss of consciousnessâyou must also report to the relevant authority. In many African countries, workplaces must report serious injuries to the labour department or OSHA. For example, in Kenya, report to the Directorate of Occupational Safety and Health Services (DOSHS). In Nigeria, report to the Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment. Check your local laws. Keep a copy of all reports for at least 5 years.

Near-misses matter too. A near-miss is when someone almost gets hurt. Write it down as well, because it shows a hazard before someone is injured. Review all reports monthly. Look for trends: are most cuts happening on Fridays? Are burns from the same stove? Then fix the problem. Share lessons with your team. Documentation shows you take safety seriously, which can reduce liability and insurance costs.

lessons.title: Legal Protections and Liability in the Workplace
lessons.body:
Many business owners and volunteers worry: if I give first aid and something goes wrong, can I be sued? In most African countries, Good Samaritan laws protect people who give emergency first aid in good faith. For example, in South Africa, the Good Samaritan principle is part of common law; in Kenya, the Occupational Safety and Health Act encourages first aid without fear of liability if done reasonably. However, protections vary. Your best protection is to act within your training, not beyond it.

What does 'within your training' mean? If you are trained in basic first aid, you can clean cuts, apply bandages, and do CPR. You should not perform surgery, give injections, or prescribe medicine. Always get consent from a conscious adult before helping. For a child, get consent from a parent or guardian if present. If the person is unconscious, consent is assumed. Do not move someone with a suspected neck or back injury unless they are in immediate danger (like fire).

Employers have a legal duty to provide a safe workplace and first aid. In many countries, this is spelled out in labour laws. For example, Kenya's OSHA 2007 requires employers to have first aid kits, trained first aiders, and to report accidents. Nigeria's Factories Act requires similar. If you fail to provide first aid and someone is harmed, you could be liable. But if you have a kit, a plan, and trained staff, you are meeting your duty.

Document everything: training records, kit checks, incident reports, and drills. This shows you took reasonable steps. Also, consider insurance. Some business insurance policies cover first aid liability. Check with your provider. Finally, never charge for first aidâit should be free. If you follow these steps, you protect both your people and your business.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Workplace and Community First Aid Preparedness

In African agribusiness and community enterprises, first aid preparedness is not only a legal obligation in many jurisdictions but a core operational risk-management function. Whether you run a grain milling operation in Nakuru, a fish processing unit in Mwanza, a cocoa buying station in Kumasi, or a farm-input retail shop in Lilongwe, the ability to respond quickly and correctly to injury or sudden illness protects lives, reduces downtime, lowers insurance exposure, and preserves your licence to operate. This module provides a practical reference framework for conducting needs assessments, building kits, developing emergency action plans, training staff and volunteers, documenting incidents, and understanding legal protections and liability.

1. Conducting a First Aid Needs Assessment

A needs assessment identifies the specific hazards, workforce size, distance to emergency services, and legal requirements that determine your first aid provision. In African agribusiness settings, common hazards include machinery entanglement (maize shellers, cassava graters, fish smokers), chemical exposure (pesticides, fertilisers, fumigants), burns (processing units, welding), snake bites and scorpion stings (field operations), heat stress, and road traffic incidents during produce transport. The assessment should be documented, reviewed at least annually, and updated after any incident or operational change.

Key steps: (1) list all work activities and locations; (2) identify hazards and likely injuries; (3) count workers, contractors, visitors, and community members on site; (4) measure distance and travel time to the nearest clinic or hospital; (5) check national occupational safety and health (OSH) regulations; (6) determine the number of trained first aiders and kits required. In many African countries, OSH laws require at least one trained first aider per 50 workers in lower-risk settings, and more in high-risk operations such as agro-processing.

Table 1: Example first aid needs assessment matrix for a mid-sized agro-processing enterprise (150 workers, 25 km from district hospital)
Hazard / Activity Likely Injury Risk Level First Aid Requirement Kit & Training Notes
Grain milling & conveyor belts Crush, amputation, cuts High Trauma kit, tourniquet, burn dressing 2 trained first aiders per shift; monthly drill
Pesticide storage & spraying Poisoning, chemical burns, eye injury High Eye wash, activated charcoal (if advised), gloves Chemical safety training; antidote protocol
Field work (harvesting, planting) Snake bite, cuts, heat stress Medium Pressure bandage, oral rehydration salts, shade Field kit per team; snake bite training
Vehicle loading & transport Fractures, head injury, bleeding Medium Vehicle kit, spinal board, reflective vest Driver first aid certification
Office & retail area Minor cuts, fainting, burns Low Basic kit, plasters, antiseptic 1 trained first aider; kit checked quarterly

Source: Adapted from ILO, Code of Practice on Safety and Health in Agriculture (2011), and Kenyaâs Occupational Safety and Health Act (OSHA), 2007, First Aid Rules.

2. Building and Maintaining a First Aid Kit

A first aid kit must match the hazards identified in the assessment. In African agribusiness, kits should be robust, dust-proof, and heat-resistant. Include supplies for bleeding control, burns, fractures, eye injuries, snake bites, and heat-related illness. Consider local availability and expiry datesâmany imported supplies expire quickly in high temperatures. Establish a named kit custodian, a checklist, and a monthly inspection routine. Replace used or expired items immediately.

Table 2: Recommended contents for a workplace first aid kit in African agribusiness (per 50 workers)
Category Item Quantity Notes
Bleeding control Sterile gauze pads (10Ã10 cm) 20 Individually wrapped
Bleeding control Crepe bandages (7.5 cm) 10 Reusable after washing
Bleeding control Tourniquet (CAT or improvised) 2 Only for life-threatening limb bleeding
Burns Burn gel dressing 5 Check expiry; store below 25Â°C
Eye injury Sterile eye wash (500 ml) 4 For chemical splash
Fractures Splints (assorted) 4 Can improvise with local materials
Snake bite Pressure immobilisation bandage 2 Do not cut or suck wound
Heat stress Oral rehydration salts (ORS) 20 sachets WHO formula
Infection control Disposable gloves (nitrile) 50 pairs Latex-free
Infection control Antiseptic wipes / solution 20 Alcohol-free for open wounds
Documentation Incident report forms 10 Waterproof folder
Communication Emergency contact list 1 Laminated, updated quarterly

Source: Adapted from WHO, International Medical Guide for Ships (3rd ed., 2007), and the American Red Cross, First Aid/CPR/AED Participantâs Manual (2021), contextualised for African agribusiness by the author.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Snake Bite and Chemical Exposure:

Do not cut, suck, or apply ice to a snake bite. Do not use a tourniquet on a snake bite. Immobilise the limb, keep the person calm, and transport to hospital immediately. For chemical exposure, remove contaminated clothing, flush the area with clean water for at least 20 minutes, and consult the pesticide label or poison control centre. Never induce vomiting after ingesting a chemical unless specifically instructed by a medical professional. In remote areas, pre-identify the nearest antivenom and poison treatment centre before an incident occurs.

3. Developing Emergency Action Plans

An Emergency Action Plan (EAP) is a written document that outlines what to do when an incident occurs. It must be specific to your site, accessible to all workers, and practised regularly. Key components: emergency contacts (ambulance, police, local clinic, poison control), evacuation routes and assembly points, roles and responsibilities (first aider, incident commander, communications officer), transport arrangements, and post-incident procedures. In rural African settings, where ambulance response may be delayed or unavailable, the EAP should include a designated vehicle and driver, a pre-arranged route to the nearest hospital, and a communication tree using mobile phones or radio.

4. Training and Drills for Staff and Volunteers

Training must be practical, culturally appropriate, and repeated. At minimum, all staff should receive basic first aid awareness, while designated first aiders should complete a certified course (e.g., Red Cross, St John Ambulance, or national OSH authority). Drills should be conducted at least twice a year and should simulate realistic scenarios: a machinery amputation, a snake bite in the field, a chemical splash, or a vehicle accident during transport. After each drill, conduct a debrief and update the EAP. Keep training records for legal compliance.

5. Incident Reporting and Documentation

Every incidentâeven a near missâmust be recorded. Documentation serves four purposes: (1) legal compliance and insurance claims; (2) identifying trends and preventing recurrence; (3) supporting workersâ compensation; (4) demonstrating due diligence. Use a standard incident report form that captures date, time, location, persons involved, injury description, first aid given, outcome, and corrective actions. Store records securely for the period required by national law (often 3â5 years). In many African jurisdictions, failure to report a serious workplace injury can result in fines or licence suspension.

6. Legal Protections and Liability in the Workplace

Employers in most African countries have a legal duty to provide a safe working environment and adequate first aid under OSH legislation (e.g., Kenyaâs OSHA 2007, Nigeriaâs Factories Act, South Africaâs OHS Act 85 of 1993, Ghanaâs Labour Act 2003). This includes providing trained first aiders, kits, and emergency procedures. Liability can arise from negligence, failure to train, or inadequate equipment. However, many jurisdictions also provide âGood Samaritanâ protections for voluntary first aiders acting in good faith. Businesses should verify their national laws and consider first aid provision as both a legal obligation and a reputational asset. Documenting training, kit inspections, and incident reports demonstrates due diligence and can reduce liability exposure.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Conduct a documented first aid needs assessment at least annually and after any major operational change.
  • Provide at least one trained first aider per 50 workers (more for high-risk operations).
  • Maintain a fully stocked, heat-resistant first aid kit in every work area and vehicle.
  • Appoint a named kit custodian and inspect kits monthly; replace expired items immediately.
  • Write and display an Emergency Action Plan with local emergency contacts and evacuation routes.
  • Run practical first aid drills twice a year and debrief with all staff and volunteers.
  • Record every incident and near miss on a standard form; review trends quarterly.
  • Verify national OSH legal requirements and keep training and inspection records for at least 3 years.

Further Reading

  • ILO Code of Practice on Safety and Health in Agriculture (2011) â free PDF, covers first aid and OSH in agriculture.
  • WHO Prehospital Emergency Care Systems (2008) â free guidance on emergency care planning.
  • American Red Cross First Aid/CPR/AED Participantâs Manual â free PDF, practical first aid reference.
  • ILO NATLEX Database of National Labour, Social Security and Related Human Rights Legislation â search your countryâs OSH laws.
  • WHO Africa â Emergency Care Resources â regional guidance and tools.

quiz.q: What is the first step in conducting a first aid needs assessment?
options: A) Buy a first aid kit
B) Walk through your site and list hazards
C) Train all staff in CPR
quiz.explanation: The assessment starts by identifying hazards and who is at risk.

quiz.q: In Kenya, which law requires workplaces to have first aid?
quiz.explanation: The Occupational Safety and Health Act (OSHA) 2007 requires first aid provisions.

quiz.q: How often should you review your first aid needs assessment?
options: C) Every year or when activities change
D) Only when an incident occurs
quiz.explanation: An annual review or when operations change keeps the assessment current.

quiz.q: What is a recommended number of trained first aiders for 50 employees?
quiz.explanation: For every 50 employees, at least one trained first aider is recommended, but two ensures coverage.

quiz.q: Which item is essential for a first aid kit in a chemical workplace?
quiz.explanation: Eye wash is critical for chemical splashes to the eyes.

quiz.q: How often should you check your first aid kit inventory?
quiz.explanation: A monthly check ensures supplies are stocked and not expired.

quiz.q: Why should you store your first aid kit in a cool, dry place?
options: B) To prevent supplies from degrading
quiz.explanation: Heat and humidity can ruin items like gloves, ointments, and bandages.

quiz.q: What should you do after using an item from the first aid kit?
options: B) Write it in a log sheet
quiz.explanation: You should log the use and restock the item.

quiz.q: What does an Emergency Action Plan (EAP) include?
options: B) Steps for response, roles, and communication
quiz.explanation: An EAP covers who does what, how to call for help, and where to meet.

quiz.q: In an emergency, who should meet the ambulance?
quiz.explanation: A guide directs emergency services to the scene quickly.

quiz.q: How often should you practise your Emergency Action Plan?
quiz.explanation: Quarterly drills keep the plan fresh and effective.

quiz.q: What should you do if phone networks are down during an emergency?
options: B) Use a runner and meet at a pre-agreed point
D) Drive to the clinic yourself
quiz.explanation: Having a backup communication plan is essential.

quiz.q: How often should you review your EAP after a real incident?
quiz.explanation: Reviewing immediately allows you to improve the plan based on lessons learned.

quiz.q: What percentage of your team should ideally be trained in first aid?
quiz.explanation: At least 10% is a good minimum, more for high-risk settings.

quiz.q: Which organisation offers first aid training in many African countries?
quiz.explanation: National Red Cross societies provide first aid training.

quiz.q: What is a drill?
options: B) A practice of your emergency plan
C) A type of first aid kit
quiz.explanation: A drill is a simulation to practise emergency response.

quiz.q: How long should a basic first aid course last?
quiz.explanation: A good basic course includes hands-on practice and lasts at least 6-8 hours.

quiz.q: What should you do after a drill?
options: B) Discuss what went well and what to improve
quiz.explanation: A debrief helps identify strengths and areas for improvement.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an incident report?
options: B) To learn and improve safety
quiz.explanation: Incident reports help identify trends and prevent future injuries.

quiz.q: How soon after an incident should you fill out a report?
options: D) At the end of the year
quiz.explanation: Prompt reporting ensures accurate details.

quiz.q: What is a near-miss?
options: B) An event that almost caused injury
D) A type of first aid
quiz.explanation: A near-miss is a close call that could have caused harm.

quiz.q: Why should you report a near-miss?
options: B) To identify hazards before someone is hurt
quiz.explanation: Near-miss reports reveal hazards that can be fixed.

quiz.q: How long should you keep incident reports?
quiz.explanation: Many laws require keeping records for at least 5 years.

quiz.q: In Kenya, which authority should serious workplace injuries be reported to?
quiz.explanation: The Directorate of Occupational Safety and Health Services (DOSHS) handles workplace incidents.

quiz.q: What does a Good Samaritan law protect?
options: A) People who give first aid in good faith
B) People who charge for first aid
C) People who refuse to help
D) People who cause harm intentionally
quiz.explanation: Good Samaritan laws protect those who help in an emergency without expecting reward.

quiz.q: What should you do before giving first aid to a conscious adult?
quiz.explanation: Consent respects the person's rights and is legally required.

quiz.q: What is the legal duty of employers regarding first aid?
options: B) To provide a safe workplace and first aid
C) Only to call an ambulance
D) To train all staff in surgery
quiz.explanation: Employers must provide first aid kits, trained staff, and a safe environment.

quiz.q: Why is documentation important for legal protection?
options: A) It shows you took reasonable steps
quiz.explanation: Records of training, kit checks, and incidents demonstrate due diligence.

quiz.q: What should you never do when giving first aid?
options: C) Apply pressure to a bleed
quiz.explanation: First aiders should only act within their training; surgery is not first aid.

quiz.q: Should you charge for first aid?
options: B) Only if the person can pay
C) No, it should be free
quiz.explanation: First aid is a humanitarian act and should not be charged for.
